Many non-Christians joined the churches, and church membership grew substantially in the following years.

Khasi Christians, like the Welsh, expressed the revival above all through hymns and prayer. Missionaries reported that ordinary believers, including women and young people, prayed aloud in meetings for the first time, and that local evangelists went out to villages that had not yet heard the gospel. The revival also strengthened the use of the Khasi language in worship and print, and helped train a generation of Khasi pastors and elders who would lead the church as the missionary era ended.

In 1906 the General Assembly of the Khasi-Jaintia churches met at Mairang. Among those who attended were Christians from the Lushai Hills (now Mizoram), where the church was still small after mission work by Baptists and Welsh Presbyterians since the 1890s. According to Mizo church tradition, they were deeply moved by what they saw at Mairang and on their return home in 1906 revival broke out among the Mizo, with prayer, confession and fervent song.

The Mizo revival of 1906 was the first of several waves (others followed around 1913, 1919 and the 1930s). Later revivals developed a distinctive Mizo style, with drum-accompanied songs in local tunes, dance (sometimes in a circle) and visions, which missionaries at first resisted and then largely accepted. Within half a century, most Mizo people had become Christians.

The revivals of 1905-1906 are remembered in north-east India as the time when Christianity became truly local. Khasi and Mizo leaders took increasing responsibility, and the Presbyterian churches of Meghalaya and Mizoram became among the largest Christian bodies in India, sending their own missionaries in later decades.

keyMoments.text: Thomas Jones begins the Welsh mission in the Khasi Hills.
News of the Welsh Revival reaches the Khasi churches; special prayer meetings begin.
Revival breaks out at a presbytery gathering and spreads through the Khasi and Jaintia Hills.
Mizo Christians attend the Khasi General Assembly at Mairang.
Revival begins in the Lushai (Mizo) Hills on their return.
Further waves of Mizo revival develop indigenous song and dance.

experiences.significance: The 1905-1906 revivals are a clear example of the Welsh Revival's global reach and a turning point in the Christianisation of north-east India, where Meghalaya, Mizoram and Nagaland now have Christian majorities. They show how revival accelerated the shift from missionary-led churches to indigenous leadership, worship and music. They also raised enduring questions, still debated in Indian and global missiology, about how far local cultural forms should shape Christian worship.

experiences.title: The Valparaíso revival and the birth of Chilean Pentecostalism
experiences.account: After reading Minnie Abrams' booklet on the Mukti revival in India, the American Methodist missionary Willis C. Hoover and his wife Mary Louise led their Valparaíso congregation in prayer for a new outpouring of the Spirit. In 1909 the church experienced tongues, visions, falling, laughter, dancing and weeping. Methodist leaders and the press criticised the movement; in 1910 the Methodist Annual Conference judged its teachings unscriptural, and Hoover and his followers left to form the Iglesia Metodista Pentecostal, the root of most Chilean Pentecostalism.

primarySource.title: Willis C. Hoover, Historia del Avivamiento Pentecostal en Chile
primarySource.citation: W.C. Hoover, Historia del Avivamiento Pentecostal en Chile (Valparaíso, 1931; Eng. trans. M. Hoover, 2000)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Hoover believed he was seeing the same Pentecost reported in India and Los Angeles; his Methodist superiors called the movement 'anti-Methodist, contrary to Scripture and irrational', and Chilean newspapers mocked it.

assessments.text: Chilean Pentecostals regard 1909 as their Pentecost, an independent, Latin American outpouring of the Spirit that produced a church led by working-class Chileans with Methodist roots and Pentecostal fervour.
Methodist historians recognise Hoover's sincerity and the revival's Methodist roots, while noting the conflict over order, doctrine and the role of ecstatic experience in the 1910 schism.
Catholic observers long viewed Pentecostal growth in Chile as a challenge; more recently, Catholic scholars and the charismatic renewal have studied its appeal among the poor.

Scholars (e.g. Allan Anderson, Juan Sepúlveda) stress that Chilean Pentecostalism arose from global networks (Mukti, Azusa) but grew as an autonomous, indigenous movement without North American Pentecostal missionaries.

debates: Order and ecstasy in Methodist worship.
Global connections versus local origins of Latin American Pentecostalism.
Pentecostalism's appeal among the urban poor.
experiences.story:
Willis Collins Hoover was born in Freeport, Illinois, in 1858 and trained as a physician before going to Chile in 1889 as a teacher with the Methodist missions begun by William Taylor. He became pastor of the Methodist Episcopal church in Valparaíso, a busy port city with many poor and working-class people. Chilean Protestantism was small, and Methodism there was largely led by foreigners.

In 1907 Hoover's wife, Mary Louise, received from a former classmate, Minnie Abrams, a booklet called The Baptism of the Holy Ghost and Fire. Abrams was a missionary with Pandita Ramabai at Mukti in India, and her booklet described the revival there in 1905-1906, with confession, visions and tongues. The Hoovers also learned of the events at Azusa Street in Los Angeles. They asked their congregation to pray for revival and to study the book of Acts.

Prayer meetings grew from 1907 into 1909, with night vigils and Bible study. According to Hoover's later history, in 1909 the meetings changed: people wept, laughed, fell to the floor, danced, spoke in tongues and reported visions and dreams; some, previously drunkards or violent men, became preachers. Members went out into the streets and visited other Methodist congregations in Santiago, where similar scenes occurred.

The movement provoked strong reactions. Valparaíso newspapers ridiculed the meetings, police were called, and some members were arrested for disturbing the peace. Other Methodist pastors and missionaries feared disorder and false teaching. When the Methodist Annual Conference met in February 1910, it formally rejected the movement's teachings as contrary to Scripture and to Methodism, and Hoover was effectively forced out.

In April 1910 Hoover and the members who followed him, together with congregations in Santiago, organised the Iglesia Metodista Pentecostal (Methodist Pentecostal Church). It kept Methodist structures such as episcopal leadership and infant baptism, while making the Pentecostal experience central. It was led and financed by Chileans themselves, used street preaching, and trained pastors 'on the job' rather than in seminaries.

The style of the new church was distinctive. Services combined Methodist hymns with spontaneous prayer, testimonies, tongues and what Chileans called 'the dance of the Spirit'. Every member was expected to witness, and street preaching with small bands became a familiar sight in Chilean towns. Pastors usually rose from among working-class members through years of practical service. Historians have noted the parallel with the Brazilian Assemblies of God founded at Belém in 1911, and with other movements that grew from the same global news of revival.

Later divisions, including a 1933 split that produced the Iglesia Evangélica Pentecostal, multiplied Pentecostal denominations. By the 2002 census Protestants, the large majority of them Pentecostal, made up roughly 15 per cent of Chile's population. Hoover died in Valparaíso in 1936, and his Historia del Avivamiento Pentecostal en Chile (1931) remains the main early source for the revival.

keyMoments.text: Willis Hoover arrives in Chile as a Methodist missionary teacher.
Minnie Abrams' booklet on the Mukti revival reaches the Hoovers; the Valparaíso church starts praying for revival.
Revival breaks out in Valparaíso with tongues, visions and other manifestations; it spreads to Santiago.
The Methodist Annual Conference rejects the movement.
Hoover and his followers form the Iglesia Metodista Pentecostal.
Hoover publishes his history of the revival.
A split produces the Iglesia Evangélica Pentecostal.

experiences.significance: Valparaíso 1909 is one of the founding events of Latin American Pentecostalism, a movement that has reshaped the religious map of the continent. It shows how revival news travelled from India and Los Angeles to South America, and how Pentecostalism grew quickly once led by local people from the working classes. The schism with Methodism also illustrates recurring tensions between established Protestant churches and Spirit-centred movements.

experiences.title: The Shantung Revival (1927-1937)
experiences.account: From 1927 the Norwegian Lutheran missionary Marie Monsen, insisting on the question 'Have you been born again?', preached among missionaries and Chinese Christians in Shandong. Southern Baptist missionaries at Huangxian (Hwanghsien), including Charles and Ola Culpepper, reported confession, restitution and a healing of Ola Culpepper's eye after prayer. By 1930-1932 a revival marked by deep conviction, public confession, joyful worship, and among some groups tongues and visions, spread through Baptist, Presbyterian and other churches in Shandong, until the Japanese invasion of 1937.

primarySource.title: Mary K. Crawford, The Shantung Revival; Marie Monsen, The Awakening
primarySource.citation: M.K. Crawford, The Shantung Revival (Shanghai, 1933); M. Monsen, The Awakening: Revival in China 1927-1937 (Eng. trans. London, 1961)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Missionaries and Chinese leaders saw the revival as a long-prayed-for work of the Spirit; some missionaries, especially those uneasy about Pentecostal elements, criticised the more ecstatic groups such as the Spiritual Gifts Society.

assessments.text: Southern Baptists remember the revival as a model of renewal through repentance, the new birth and prayer; Bertha Smith and C.L. Culpepper popularised it in the United States.
Pentecostal historians highlight the tongues, healings and Spirit-filling in parts of the revival, and its links to Chinese indigenous movements.

Chinese Christians see the revival, with John Sung's later campaigns and indigenous groups like the Jesus Family, as a key step towards a self-propagating Chinese church that later survived persecution.
Daniel Bays and others situate the revival in a time of war, banditry and anti-foreign nationalism, when missionaries' authority was weakened and Chinese leaders gained a larger role.

debates: Emphasis on the new birth among missionaries and church members.
Ecstatic and charismatic phenomena versus order.
Missionary-led versus indigenous Chinese revival.
experiences.story:
In the 1920s Shandong province in north China was a centre of Protestant missions, with American Southern Baptists, Presbyterians and others running schools, hospitals and churches. It was also a region of warlords, banditry and famine, and in 1927 the Nationalist advance and anti-foreign violence forced many missionaries to retreat to the coastal port of Chefoo (Yantai). Many of them were discouraged by churches that seemed to have members without spiritual life.

Marie Monsen, born in Norway in 1878, had served in China since 1901 with the Norwegian Lutheran China Mission. She had prayed for many years for revival and, according to her later account, came to believe that many professing Christians, including missionaries, had never been truly born again. In 1927 she spoke to missionaries gathered at Chefoo and elsewhere, asking direct questions: had they been born again, had they been filled with the Spirit, was there unconfessed sin in their lives?

Among those who heard her were Southern Baptist missionaries from Huangxian (Hwanghsien), including Charles Culpepper and his wife Ola. Ola Culpepper suffered from a serious eye problem; according to C.L. Culpepper's later account, after Monsen and others prayed and anointed her with oil, she was healed. This event and the conviction produced by Monsen's questioning led missionaries to confess sins to one another and to Chinese colleagues, including attitudes of superiority.

From about 1930 revival spread among Chinese believers in Huangxian and throughout Shandong. Meetings were marked by deep conviction, often with people falling, weeping or crying out, followed by public confession and restitution, and then by joy, praise and long hours of prayer. Students in mission schools were deeply affected. Some groups reported tongues, visions and healings, and an independent Spiritual Gifts Society emerged with more ecstatic practices, which many missionaries considered extreme.

Chinese evangelists became central. John Sung, the scientist turned preacher, held campaigns in Shandong in the early 1930s that drew thousands. Indigenous communities such as the Jesus Family, founded by Jing Dianying at Mazhuang in Shandong in 1927, combined revival piety with communal living. Mary Crawford's The Shantung Revival (1933) collected testimonies, and Monsen's own account, The Awakening, appeared later.

Many missionaries described the revival as having changed their own lives. Bertha Smith, a Southern Baptist missionary in Shandong, later told in her memoir Go Home and Tell (1965) how she was convicted of pride and lack of love towards Chinese co-workers and found new freedom in prayer. Chinese pastors and evangelists, too, confessed rivalries and hidden sins, and some churches became self-supporting and began sending their own preachers into the countryside.

The revival waned with the Japanese invasion of 1937 and the war that followed. Monsen left China in the early 1930s and died in Norway in 1962. After 1949 the missionaries left China, but many of the Chinese Christians shaped by the revival led churches through the following decades of hardship.

keyMoments.text: Marie Monsen arrives in China as a Lutheran missionary.
Anti-foreign unrest drives missionaries to Chefoo; Monsen's preaching on the new birth begins to stir them.
Ola Culpepper's eye is reported healed after prayer, and missionaries begin confessing sins.
Revival spreads among Chinese believers in Huangxian and across Shandong.
Peak of the revival; John Sung holds campaigns in Shandong.
Mary Crawford publishes The Shantung Revival.
The Japanese invasion brings the revival period to an end.

experiences.significance: The Shantung Revival is one of the most important revivals in modern Chinese Christianity, and it helped shift leadership towards Chinese evangelists and indigenous movements before the missionary era ended in 1949-1951. Its emphasis on new birth, confession and the Spirit influenced Southern Baptist and evangelical piety in the West through books by C.L. Culpepper and Bertha Smith. Historians see it as part of the roots of the vigorous Chinese Protestant movement that later grew under Communist rule.

experiences.title: The Lewis (Hebrides) Revival, 1949-1952
experiences.account: In the parish of Barvas on the Isle of Lewis, two elderly sisters, Peggy and Christine Smith, and a group of men praying in a barn sought revival through 1949. The parish minister, James Murray MacKay, invited the Faith Mission evangelist Duncan Campbell, who arrived in December 1949. Meetings soon lasted late into the night, with deep conviction, weeping, some people falling or trembling, and many conversions, especially among young people; the movement spread to other villages and islands until about 1952.

primarySource.title: Duncan Campbell, The Lewis Awakening 1949-1953
primarySource.citation: D. Campbell, The Lewis Awakening 1949-1953 (Edinburgh: Faith Mission, 1954); later sermons and recorded addresses

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Supporters saw a sovereign work of God in answer to prayer; Free Church of Scotland leaders in Lewis and others were critical, objecting to Campbell's theology and to physical manifestations, and the revival became a source of local controversy.

assessments.text: The Lewis Awakening is cited worldwide as a classic case of revival born of persistent prayer, with conviction of sin and community transformation.
Some Highland Presbyterians were wary of Campbell's Arminian-leaning Faith Mission theology, of emotional and physical phenomena, and of outsiders claiming credit for local spiritual life.
Charismatic writers draw on Campbell's accounts of physical manifestations and of the sense of God's presence, though Campbell himself was not Pentecostal and did not endorse tongues.

Researchers note that many popular stories come from Campbell's later retellings, which sometimes compress or embellish events; local oral histories confirm a significant awakening but with more varied perspectives.

debates: The reliability of Campbell's later retellings.
Free Church opposition and Highland church tensions.
Prayer and divine sovereignty in revival theology.
experiences.story:
The Isle of Lewis, in the Outer Hebrides off north-west Scotland, was a Gaelic-speaking crofting and fishing community with a strong Presbyterian tradition and a history of earlier revivals. After the Second World War many people, especially the young, had drifted from church life; dances and drinking were popular, and ministers worried about spiritual decline. According to later accounts, church leaders on the island called for prayer about the state of religion.

In the parish of Barvas, two elderly sisters, Peggy Smith (aged 84 and blind) and Christine Smith (82 and bent with arthritis), unable to attend church, prayed in their cottage for revival, holding to Isaiah 44:3 ('I will pour water upon him that is thirsty'). According to accounts later told by Campbell, Peggy had a dream that the church would be crowded with young people. At the same time a group of men, including church elders, met to pray in a barn several nights a week. Their minister, the Rev. James Murray MacKay of the Church of Scotland, invited an evangelist to lead a mission.

The evangelist was Duncan Campbell, a Gaelic speaker from Argyll who had served in the First World War and worked for many years with the Faith Mission, an interdenominational holiness organisation. He arrived in December 1949. The first meetings were ordinary, but soon, according to Campbell and others, a powerful sense of God's presence came over the community. After one late meeting, people gathered around the church and nearby houses, and many went in to pray; services continued into the early morning.

Witnesses describe people weeping, crying out, sometimes falling or trembling, and coming under deep conviction of sin, even outside meetings, while working in the fields or on the roads. Young people who had been at a dance in the parish hall are said to have left it to go to the church. Campbell later described a prayer meeting at Arnol when, he said, the house shook. Within weeks hundreds professed conversion, and meetings were held across Lewis, then in Harris, North Uist and Berneray.

The movement provoked controversy. Leaders of the Free Church of Scotland in Lewis publicly criticised the mission, objecting among other things to Campbell's theology and methods. Some in the community found the physical manifestations disturbing. Supporters pointed to changed lives, new elders and ministers, and reduced drinking. Campbell continued visiting the islands until about 1952-1953.

Campbell became principal of the Faith Mission Bible College in Edinburgh and spoke widely in Britain, North America and elsewhere about the Lewis Awakening until his death in Switzerland in 1972. His recorded addresses spread the story around the world. Later historians and local people have noted that some of his retellings simplified or heightened events, but they agree that Lewis experienced a genuine and memorable awakening.

The revival period ends; Campbell publishes The Lewis Awakening.

experiences.significance: The Lewis Awakening is one of the most widely told revival stories of the twentieth century, used by evangelicals and charismatics around the world to encourage prayer for revival. It also shows the tensions between different Presbyterian traditions in the Scottish Highlands and the risks of revival stories growing in the retelling. Historians use it as a case study of how local experience becomes global legend.

experiences.title: The Duquesne Weekend and the Catholic Charismatic Renewal

place.name: The Ark and the Dove retreat house, Gibsonia, Pennsylvania

experiences.account: On 17-19 February 1967, about twenty-five students from Duquesne University, Pittsburgh, attended a retreat on the first chapters of Acts at The Ark and the Dove retreat house near Gibsonia. Several faculty members had recently experienced 'baptism in the Holy Spirit' at an interdenominational prayer meeting. On the Saturday evening, students who went into the chapel experienced a powerful sense of God's presence; many prayed for hours, wept, laughed and some spoke in tongues. The experience spread to Notre Dame and Michigan State within weeks and became the Catholic Charismatic Renewal.

primarySource.title: Kevin and Dorothy Ranaghan, Catholic Pentecostals; Patti Gallagher Mansfield, As By a New Pentecost
primarySource.citation: K. and D. Ranaghan, Catholic Pentecostals (Paramus, NJ, 1969); P. Gallagher Mansfield, As By a New Pentecost (1992)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Participants saw it as a 'new Pentecost', in the language of Pope John XXIII's prayer for the Second Vatican Council; some bishops and theologians were cautious, and Pentecostals and evangelicals were surprised to find the experience among Catholics.

assessments.text: The Renewal has received papal support from Paul VI (1975) to Francis, who described it as a 'current of grace'; it is integrated into Catholic life through prayer groups, covenant communities and CHARIS, while bishops urge discernment and ecclesial obedience.
Many Pentecostals welcomed it as proof that the Spirit's outpouring crossed denominational lines, though some were puzzled that Catholics kept Marian devotion and the sacraments.
Some traditionalists criticise the Renewal as importing Protestant Pentecostal theology and emotional worship into the liturgy.
Cessationist and some evangelical critics question the experience on doctrinal grounds, seeing Catholic teaching on grace and the sacraments as unchanged.
Scholars place the weekend in the ferment after Vatican II and the 1960s; the Renewal became one of the largest Catholic movements, though estimates of participants vary widely.

debates: Baptism in the Spirit and sacramental theology.
Ecumenism with Pentecostals.
Authority and covenant communities (some faced abuse and control problems).
experiences.story:
The Second Vatican Council (1962-1965) had ended only a year before, and many Catholics were seeking renewal. Pope John XXIII had prayed that the Council would be like 'a new Pentecost'. At Duquesne University, a Catholic university in Pittsburgh run by the Spiritans, two lay theology instructors, Ralph Keifer and Patrick Bourgeois, involved in the Cursillo movement, were longing for a deeper experience of the Holy Spirit. They had read two books popular among Protestant charismatics: David Wilkerson's The Cross and the Switchblade and John Sherrill's They Speak with Other Tongues.

In January 1967 they attended an interdenominational charismatic prayer meeting at the home of a Protestant laywoman, Florence Dodge, in the Pittsburgh area. There they asked for prayer to receive the baptism in the Holy Spirit, and some began to speak in tongues. They then planned a weekend retreat for students from the university's Chi Rho Society, asking participants to prepare by reading the first four chapters of Acts and The Cross and the Switchblade.

On Friday 17 February 1967, about twenty-five students arrived at The Ark and the Dove, a retreat house in Gibsonia, north of Pittsburgh. The talks dealt with the Holy Spirit and Pentecost. On Saturday evening a birthday party had been planned for some of the participants. One student, Patti Gallagher, went into the chapel, intending to ask others to join the party; according to her account, she felt overwhelmed by God's presence and found herself kneeling and then lying prostrate before the tabernacle.

Over the following hours other students came into the chapel, one after another, and experienced similar things. Some wept, others laughed, many prayed for hours, and several began to speak in tongues without anyone having laid hands on them. Others were prayed for by the faculty members. Participants later described the night as 'a new Pentecost' and their experience as baptism in the Spirit.

News spread quickly through Catholic networks. In early March 1967, a group at the University of Notre Dame, including Kevin and Dorothy Ranaghan, had similar experiences, and within weeks a group at Michigan State University followed. In April 1967 the first national gathering took place at Notre Dame, and the Ranaghans' book Catholic Pentecostals (1969) introduced the movement widely. Covenant communities such as the Word of God in Ann Arbor formed.

Church leaders responded with caution, then increasing support. Cardinal Léon-Joseph Suenens became an important advocate, and in 1975 Pope Paul VI addressed thousands of participants in Rome at Pentecost, speaking of the renewal as an opportunity for the Church while urging discernment. Popes John Paul II, Benedict XVI and Francis also supported it, and in 2017 Francis celebrated its golden jubilee in Rome. In 2019 the Vatican created CHARIS to serve the renewal worldwide.

experiences.significance: The Duquesne Weekend is usually counted as the birth of the Catholic Charismatic Renewal, which brought Pentecostal-style spirituality into the world's largest church and contributed to the global spread of charismatic Christianity, especially in Latin America, Africa and Asia. It opened new ecumenical contact between Catholics and Pentecostals, including a formal international dialogue since 1972. Critics within and outside the Catholic Church raised concerns about theology, emotionalism and some authoritarian covenant communities, but the renewal remains a major current in global Catholicism.

experiences.title: Our Lady of Akita: messages and the weeping statue

place.name: Convent of the Handmaids of the Eucharist, Yuzawadai, Akita, Japan

experiences.account: In 1973 Sister Agnes Katsuko Sasagawa, a profoundly deaf member of the Handmaids of the Eucharist at Yuzawadai near Akita, reported light from the tabernacle, a painful cross-shaped wound on her left palm, and three messages from a wooden statue of Mary (6 July, 3 August and 13 October 1973). The third warned of a punishment of fire if humanity did not repent and of division in the Church. Between 1975 and 1981 the statue was reported to weep 101 times, observed by many visitors. In 1984 Bishop John Shojiro Ito of Niigata declared the events supernatural in origin.

primarySource.title: Bishop John Shojiro Ito, Pastoral Letter on the events at Akita (22 April 1984)
primarySource.citation: Pastoral letter of the Bishop of Niigata, 22 April 1984; account in T. Yasuda, Akita: The Tears and Message of Mary (Eng. trans. 1989)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: The local bishop investigated over many years and approved the events; others, including a first commission that was negative, doubted, and the Holy See has made no formal public judgement.

assessments.text: Approved by the local bishop, Akita is seen as a call to prayer, penance and Eucharistic adoration; the messages are read as warnings about the Church's divisions and as linked to Fatima.
Many Catholic theologians stress that private revelations, even approved ones, never bind belief, and that the apocalyptic message must be read with care.
Most Protestants regard Marian apparitions as unnecessary or as distracting from Christ, and question the messages' theology, though some respect the sincerity of the sisters.
Sceptics suggest natural or human causes for the weeping and wounds; laboratory tests reported by supporters (human blood, tears and sweat of different blood groups) have been debated.

debates: The status of the 1984 episcopal approval and the Holy See's silence.
The meaning of the apocalyptic third message and its relation to Fatima.
Testing of fluids and verification of the reported healing of deafness.
experiences.story:
Christianity in Japan has a dramatic history, from the mission of Francis Xavier in 1549 through centuries of persecution to the 'hidden Christians' who emerged in the nineteenth century. In the twentieth century Catholics remained a very small minority. In 1973 a small community of women, the Institute of the Handmaids of the Eucharist (Seitai Hoshi-kai), lived at Yuzawadai in the hills outside the northern city of Akita, under the guidance of Bishop John Shojiro Ito of Niigata.

Sister Agnes Katsuko Sasagawa, born in 1931, had suffered serious illness after surgery as a young woman and had become a Catholic after a long recovery. In early 1973 she lost her hearing completely and joined the community at Akita. On 12 June 1973, according to the community's account, she saw a brilliant light coming from the tabernacle during prayer. Soon after, a painful wound in the shape of a cross appeared on the palm of her left hand. At about the same time, sisters reported that a wooden statue of Mary in the chapel, carved by the sculptor Saburo Wakasa, showed a bleeding wound on its right hand.

On 6 July 1973, Sister Agnes said she heard a voice from the statue speaking to her, asking her to pray in reparation for the sins of the world and for priests. A second message followed on 3 August. On 13 October 1973, the anniversary of the last Fatima apparition, she reported the third: if people did not repent, a punishment greater than the flood would come, with fire falling from the sky, and the work of the devil would infiltrate even the Church, so that cardinals would oppose cardinals and bishops oppose bishops. The message called people to pray the Rosary.

From 4 January 1975 to 15 September 1981 the statue was reported to shed tears 101 times, witnessed by sisters, visitors and local people; one occasion was reportedly filmed by Japanese television. Bishop Ito, who witnessed the weeping himself, had samples tested; according to reports supporters later published, a forensic laboratory found human blood, tears and sweat. Sister Agnes reported that her hearing was restored in 1982, and other healings were claimed.

A first investigative commission in 1979 was negative, but Bishop Ito continued to study the events. On 22 April 1984, after consultations in Rome, he issued a pastoral letter recognising the supernatural character of the events and permitting veneration of Our Lady of Akita in his diocese. Some reports later claimed that Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger personally regarded the messages as reliable, but no formal Vatican judgement was published.

Akita became a place of pilgrimage for Catholics from Japan and abroad, and the third message has been widely quoted in debates about crisis in the Church. Sister Agnes lived quietly with her community, avoiding publicity.

experiences.significance: Akita is the most famous Marian apparition in Asia and one of the few in the late twentieth century to receive local episcopal approval. Its message of repentance and warning has been widely used by Catholics concerned about crisis in the Church, and it connects Japanese Catholic piety with global Marian devotion linked to Fatima. Its status shows the Catholic Church's distinction between local approval, papal silence and the non-binding character of private revelation.

experiences.title: The Kibeho apparitions in Rwanda
experiences.account: On 28 November 1981 Alphonsine Mumureke, a student at Kibeho College, a girls' secondary school in southern Rwanda, said that the Virgin Mary appeared to her, calling herself 'Nyina wa Jambo' (Mother of the Word). Anathalie Mukamazimpaka and Marie Claire Mukangango later reported apparitions too. The visions, often seen by crowds as the girls fell into ecstasy, called for prayer and repentance. On 15 August 1982 the visionaries wept and described terrifying scenes of rivers of blood and abandoned bodies, which many later read as a warning of the 1994 genocide. In 2001 Bishop Augustin Misago approved the apparitions to these three.

primarySource.title: Declaration of Bishop Augustin Misago of Gikongoro on the apparitions of Kibeho
primarySource.citation: Declaration on the apparitions of Kibeho (29 June 2001), with commission reports from 1982 onward

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Thousands of Rwandans flocked to Kibeho; local church authorities set up medical and theological commissions, and in 1988 Bishop Jean-Baptiste Gahamanyi authorised public devotion. Other claimed visionaries were not recognised.

assessments.text: Kibeho is the only Church-approved Marian apparition in Africa; the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Kibeho draws pilgrims who pray the Rosary of the Seven Sorrows promoted in the messages.
For many Rwandans the 1982 visions became a sorrowful prophecy, and Kibeho, where massacres occurred in 1994 and 1995, is both a place of pilgrimage and of mourning.
Protestants generally do not accept Marian apparitions but note the call to repentance in a society heading toward violence.

Some scholars point out that the 'prophecy' was read as such only after the genocide, and that the apparitions occurred in an ethnically charged context; they also note the role of the church in Rwandan politics.

debates: Reading the 1982 visions as a prophecy of the 1994 genocide.
The church's role and the trial of Bishop Misago (acquitted in 2000).
Why only three of the claimed visionaries were recognised.
experiences.story:
Rwanda in 1981 was a small, densely populated and overwhelmingly Christian country, with Catholics forming the largest church. It was ruled by President Juvénal Habyarimana, and tensions between Hutu and Tutsi, rooted in colonial and post-colonial history, lay below the surface. Kibeho, in the south near the Burundi border, had a parish and a Catholic girls' secondary school, Kibeho College.

On 28 November 1981, Alphonsine Mumureke, a sixteen-year-old student, was serving in the school refectory when, she said, she heard a voice and saw a beautiful woman who called herself 'Nyina wa Jambo', Mother of the Word. At first classmates and staff mocked her and she was teased; some suspected illness. On 12 January 1982 a second student, Anathalie Mukamazimpaka, reported apparitions, and on 2 March 1982 Marie Claire Mukangango, who had been one of the most mocking students, also began to see the Virgin.

The apparitions became public events. The visionaries would fall into ecstasy before crowds of thousands, speaking with the unseen figure, sometimes singing and sometimes lying for long periods. The messages called for prayer, repentance, fasting and humility, with warnings that the world was in danger. Marie Claire was asked to spread the Rosary of the Seven Sorrows of Mary.

Observers described dramatic scenes. According to accounts collected at the time, the visionaries sometimes fell heavily to the ground during ecstasy without injury, and Alphonsine and others reported 'mystical journeys' during which they lay motionless for many hours and later described seeing places of joy and of suffering. Doctors, priests and journalists came to observe, some sympathetic, some sceptical. The messages also spoke of the world turning away from God and asked people to love one another sincerely.

The most remembered day was 15 August 1982, the feast of the Assumption. Before a large crowd, according to witnesses and later accounts, the visionaries wept and trembled and described terrifying images: rivers of blood, people killing one another, abandoned bodies without heads, trees on fire. At the time many did not understand. After the genocide of 1994, in which perhaps 800,000 people, mostly Tutsi, were killed, many came to read these visions as a warning that went unheeded.

The Church moved carefully. In 1982 a medical commission and later a theological commission examined the visionaries. In 1988 Bishop Jean-Baptiste Gahamanyi of Butare authorised public devotion at Kibeho. Several others claimed visions, but these were not recognised. During the genocide Kibeho itself became a place of massacre: people who had fled to the church and school were killed in April 1994, and in April 1995 many displaced people were killed when soldiers cleared a camp at Kibeho.

Kibeho came under the new diocese of Gikongoro, led by Bishop Augustin Misago, who himself was arrested in 1999 on charges of complicity in the genocide and acquitted in 2000. On 29 June 2001 he declared that the apparitions to Alphonsine, Anathalie and Marie Claire were worthy of belief. The Sanctuary of Our Lady of Kibeho was built, and pilgrims come from Rwanda, Africa and beyond.

experiences.significance: Kibeho is the only Catholic Marian apparition in Africa to have received official approval, and its sanctuary is a major place of pilgrimage. Its association with the 1994 genocide gives it a unique place in Rwandan memory and in reflection on the churches' responsibility during the violence. For historians and theologians it raises hard questions about prophecy read after the event, and about how Christian devotion and national tragedy were intertwined in Rwanda.

experiences.title: Medjugorje: the 'Queen of Peace' apparitions

place.name: Podbrdo (Apparition Hill), Medjugorje, Bosnia and Herzegovina

experiences.account: On 24 June 1981 young people from the Croatian Catholic village of Medjugorje, then in Communist Yugoslavia, said they saw the Virgin Mary on the hill of Podbrdo. From 25 June six visionaries (Ivanka Ivanković, Mirjana Dragićević, Vicka Ivanković, Ivan Dragićević, Marija Pavlović and Jakov Čolo) reported daily apparitions, with messages calling for peace, conversion, prayer and fasting; some reported continuing apparitions for decades. The local bishops rejected the claims, the Yugoslav bishops (1991) found no proof of supernatural origin, and in 2024 the Holy See gave a 'nihil obstat' to the spiritual experience at Medjugorje without declaring the apparitions supernatural.

primarySource.title: Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith, Note 'The Queen of Peace' on the spiritual experience connected with Medjugorje
primarySource.citation: DDF, 'La Regina della Pace' (19 September 2024); Declaration of the Yugoslav Bishops' Conference (Zadar, 10 April 1991)

experiences.contemporaryInterpretation: Many local Catholics and Franciscan friars embraced the apparitions; Communist authorities saw them as nationalist agitation and jailed the parish priest Jozo Zovko; Bishop Pavao Žanić of Mostar eventually rejected them.

assessments.text: Millions of pilgrims report conversions, confessions and healing; for them Medjugorje is a 'confessional of the world' and a true Marian call to peace.

The 2024 note recognises abundant spiritual fruit and allows public devotion, but does not declare the apparitions supernatural and cautions about some messages; Pope Francis voiced scepticism about claims of daily apparitions.
The bishops of Mostar and some theologians see the phenomenon as linked to disputes between Franciscans and the diocese, with doubts about the visionaries' consistency and continuing messages.
Protestants generally reject Marian apparitions; Orthodox Christians in the region have viewed Medjugorje through the lens of Croatian-Catholic identity, especially during the 1990s wars.
Sceptics regard the phenomena as psychological or social, noting the long series of messages and the commercial pilgrimage economy.

debates: Authenticity of the apparitions versus the spiritual fruits.
Franciscan-diocesan conflict in Herzegovina.
The 2024 norms and what a 'nihil obstat' means.
experiences.story:
In 1981 Medjugorje was a poor, Croatian Catholic farming village in the hills of western Herzegovina, then part of Communist Yugoslavia. The region had a long and painful history, including violence during the Second World War. The parish was run by Franciscan friars, who had served Bosnian Catholics for centuries, and there was a long dispute between the Franciscans and the diocesan bishops of Mostar over who should run parishes.

On the afternoon of 24 June 1981, the feast of St John the Baptist, a group of young people walking near Podbrdo hill said they saw a luminous figure of a young woman holding a child. The next day, 25 June, six young people (Ivanka Ivanković, Mirjana Dragićević, Vicka Ivanković, Ivan Dragićević, Marija Pavlović and ten-year-old Jakov Čolo) went back and reported that the Virgin spoke with them. 25 June later became the anniversary date. Crowds grew rapidly, reaching thousands within days.

The authorities reacted strongly. Police questioned the young people, and doctors examined them. The Franciscan parish priest, Jozo Zovko, initially sceptical, came to support the visionaries; in August 1981 he was arrested and sentenced to prison for allegedly preaching against the state. The apparitions moved from the hill to the parish church. According to the visionaries, the Virgin identified herself as the 'Queen of Peace', calling people to peace, conversion, faith, prayer and fasting.

The local bishop, Pavao Žanić of Mostar, was initially open but later became convinced that the apparitions were not authentic, especially after the visionaries reportedly supported Franciscans in their dispute with him. His commission's negative conclusion was referred to the Yugoslav bishops' conference, which in 1991 declared at Zadar that it could not be affirmed that the events involved supernatural apparitions or revelations, while allowing pastoral care for pilgrims. Some visionaries said they still received daily or monthly messages, which continued for decades.

The visionaries also said they had been entrusted with 'secrets' about future events, which they claimed would be revealed at the proper time. Several married and raised families, some moved abroad, and they travelled widely to speak about the messages. Monthly messages, especially those reported by Marija Pavlović on the 25th of each month, were published and circulated worldwide, while critics questioned their repetitive content and the unprecedented length of the series.

Despite the official caution, Medjugorje became one of the largest Catholic pilgrimage sites in the world, drawing millions of visitors, including during and after the Bosnian war of 1992-1995. Many reported conversions, returning to confession, vocations and healings. Critics pointed to inconsistencies, commercialisation and problems in the conduct of some figures connected with the movement.

In 2010 Pope Benedict XVI established an international commission led by Cardinal Camillo Ruini, which reported in 2014. Pope Francis sent Archbishop Henryk Hoser as special envoy in 2017 and authorised official pilgrimages in 2019, while expressing personal doubts about continuing apparitions. In September 2024, under new norms, the Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith issued 'The Queen of Peace', granting a nihil obstat to the spiritual experience at Medjugorje and recognising its positive fruits, but explicitly without declaring the apparitions supernatural.

experiences.significance: Medjugorje is the most visited and most controversial Marian site of modern times, shaping Catholic devotion, pilgrimage and renewal movements worldwide. The long Church process around it, from local rejection to a 2024 nihil obstat without recognition of supernatural origin, illustrates the Catholic Church's evolving approach to private revelation. It also shows how apparitions become entangled in local church disputes, national identities and global religious tourism.
